newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada to ponder cultural future after WTO defeat.
newsitem.headline: Canada to ponder cultural future after WTO defeat.

text.p: Canadian Heritage Minister Sheila Copps said she would set a national round-table discussion on the future of Canada's cultural policies.
The announcement late on Thursday came a week after a World Trade Organization (WTO) panel struck down most of Ottawa's protectionist measures against Canadian editions of U.S. magazines.
The WTO decison was seen as a blow to Canada's attempts to protect itself from what it sees as a cultural invasion and a threat to its national identity from the United States.

"My goal is to build and strengthen a national consensus on how the federal government can best support and encourage Canadian cultural activity and Canada's cultural industries," Copps said in a statement.
Copps sent invitations to a number of "prominent" Canadians, who are involved in culture and communications, to participate in the discussion, which would be held in Ottawa on February 9 and 10.
"The round table will focus on the federal government's current cultural policy instruments and how they should be adapted and renewed in the longer term," Copps' office said in a news release.
Some of the protectionist measures rejected by the WTO included preferential postal rates, tariff restrictions and an 80 percent tax on advertising in special Canadian editions of U.S. magazines.
The tax, adopted in December 1995, hit the Canadian edition of Time Warner Inc's Sports Illustrated and prompted Washington to launch a WTO challenge of Ottawa's cultural policies.

On Thursday, a spokeswoman for Canadian International Trade Minister Art Eggleton said Canada would not request an interim review of the WTO ruling and would wait instead for the final report, which is due in March.
Analysts have said that Ottawa had little chance of success if it appealed the WTO decision.
Instead, they have suggested that Canada could devise new protectionist measures that might comply with world trade rules, or ignore the WTO ruling and invite Washington's retaliation.
Despite laws dating back to 1965 safeguarding Canada's publishing industry, up to 90 percent of Canada's cultural industry is dominated by U.S. films and publications, Eggleton said.
